World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Sunken trawler alerts police to alleged drug-smuggling plan
World.content:
Nine men have been charged over alleged attempts to smuggle tonnes of illicit drugs into Victoria by sea.

Police cottoned on to the plan after a trawler allegedly linked to the syndicate's plans sank in rough weather last year.

A 10-month joint operation, known as Operation Bruce Cremorne, involving Victoria Police, Australian Federal Police and Border Force culminated in the arrests of eight men in Victoria and one man in Sydney.

The men, aged between 31 and 72, face charges including conspiracy to import cocaine, trafficking methamphetamine, and firearms offences.

The arrests followed raids in Victoria in Morwell, Glenroy, Cranbourne, Cranbourne West, Cranbourne South and Greenvale, and in the Sydney suburb of St Clair.

Seven of the men face potential life sentences if convicted.

The charges relate to alleged attempts to smuggle quantities of up to 3.5 tonnes of cocaine into the country by sea.

Police said the syndicate made multiple attempts to travel into Bass Strait with the intention of receiving drug shipments from a ship passing through Australian waters.

The attempts failed and no drugs were brought onshore.

Police from multiple agencies were involved in the operation. (Supplied: Victoria Police.)

Victoria Police said the investigation into the syndicate was ongoing and further arrests had not been ruled out.

Superintendent Dave Cowan said police were concerned Australia had become a "favourable location" for organised crime syndicates.

"As is startlingly clear, the damage caused by the use of illicit substances ripples throughout the community, and it does not just affect those using the drug," he said.

" There have been many lives forever changed and ruined simply by their sheer misfortune of encountering someone who chose to take an illegal substance. "

Trawler sinking raises police suspicion

Police launched Operation Bruce Cremorne after the sinking of a trawler off the Victorian coast at Port Albert in May last year raised suspicion.

Investigators began monitoring the crew after becoming suspicious about why the vessel had travelled out to sea in bad weather without equipment usually required for commercial fishing.

Over the following months, police undertook surveillance of multiple boat crews suspected of being linked to the syndicate.

Police said local boat crews were allegedly involved in the drug importation plans. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

Police said the syndicate attempted to rendezvous with a "mother ship", with smaller vessels launched from larger ships.

AFP Detective Superintendent Ray Imbriano said it was a risky method.

"At-sea transfers are dangerous, and criminals using this smuggling method risk both their freedom and their lives," he said.

" It also risks the lives of first responders, who too often have had to save the lives of crew involved in drug retrieval. "

The Victorian men will face court on July 28 and the man arrested in Sydney will face a NSW court on May 20.

World.title: From farm to fashion festival: Indigenous designs stun on the runway
World.content:
In far-western Victoria, down a winding track amid rolling hills and glorious gum trees, something surprisingly beautiful and unexpected is happening.

So beautiful, that the creations emerging from an isolated farmhouse in the town of Pigeon Ponds recently graced the catwalk of one of the nation's premier fashion festivals.

Two-and-a-half years ago, farmer Sue McClure tried knitting scarves and blankets with indigenous art designs she found on the internet, but she "didn't feel right about it".

So Ms McClure decided to contact Warrnambool-based indigenous artist Sherry Johnstone, a Keerray Woorroong and Yorta Yorta woman.

The women met and realised they had a shared passion.

"We had a passion for the land and being mindful of our footprint on our environment as such, and caring for country," Ms Johnstone said.

Sue McClure gets to work creating one of the designs. (Supplied: Sue McClure)

"It was just a nice organic partnership that started with a bit of a collaboration and then trying some blankets and scarves with my artwork."

Ms McClure was immediately struck by Ms Johnstone's designs.

"She's a beautiful artist and she does amazing stuff," Ms McClure said.

Sherry Johnstone wearing her entry to the National Wool Museum Future in Fibres competition. (Supplied:Sue McClure)

Australian wool is important to both women — they use fine merino wool farmed in Tasmania, which is then sent to Italy for processing before being returned to Australia.

The duo's first project was to create a blanket shape, which turned into an outfit Ms Johnstone submitted to a National Wool Museum Future in Fibres competition last year.

The contest was an opportunity for new and emerging artists, making sure the principles behind their business were sustainable and part of a circular economy.

A page from Sherry Johnstone's 'lookbook' which features her designs. (Supplied: Sue McClure)

The competition attracted 150 entries from around the world.

When Ms Johnstone's outfit won second prize, one of the judges suggested they submit a 'lookbook' to the Melbourne Fashion Festival.

Neither of the women knew what a 'lookbook' was, so they googled it.

"[Sherry] came up with some brilliant ideas for 10 outfits, all based on her connection to country and her stories from her ancestors," Ms McClure said.

Ms Johnstone said she spent weeks pulling the designs together.

"I sat down for about two weeks and came up with designs mainly … inspired by lands … things like banksias and flowering gum … even a bit of bark that I found in a paddock," she said.

The lookbook was submitted in October and accepted into the festival in November.

Inspired by a wedge-tailed eagle 'Oh My Bundjil God' featured in the Beyond Blak Runway. (Supplied: Melbourne Fashion Festival)

Sherry Johnstone's Healing Country designs are inspired by the landscape around her. (Supplied: Melbourne Fashion Festival, Event Gallery and Mob In Fashion)

Ms McClure then had to work out how to knit the designs with a machine she had purchased from Japan in 2021.

Measuring 4.5 metres long, 1.5 metres wide and standing around 2 metres tall, the $180,000 knitting machine can produce a whole garment or knit together a piece of fabric that can be cut and sewn together.

Then the work really began, Ms Johnstone said.

"Poor Sue had a bit of pressure on her to actually create the designs for me," she said.

The pair engaged Rod Murray, a Melbourne expert in knitting software, to program the machine to turn the designs into reality.

Then, it took a week to make samples of the designs and another month to create the clothing for the fashion festival.

Sue McClure converted a shed to fit her huge knitting machine. (Supplied: Sue McClure)

But a day before the clothes were due in Melbourne, the power went out at the Pigeon Ponds farm, so Ms McClure couldn't use her sewing machine to stitch the final designs together.

"I had to do the final stitching by hand out on the verandah, in the afternoon light," Ms McClure said.

"It's certainly not just, you know, putting a couple of bits of cotton fabric together," Ms Johnstone said.

The bespoke garments finally hit the Melbourne Fashion Festival catwalk in February, as part of the Beyond Blak Runway.

"You know, we would be happy to reproduce them, if somebody was particularly interested in one," Ms Johnstone said.

Sherry Johnstone and Sue McClure at the Melbourne Fashion Festival. (Supplied: Sue McClure)

The collaboration between the women has led to a new business venture for Ms Johnstone, who started her own brand, Flash 1A, designing jumpers, hoodies, ponchos and dresses which will be produced on Ms McClure's farm, on her knitting machine.

"[It's] a reference to when mobs playfully sort of say, 'Oh, that's a Flash 1A'," Ms Johnstone said.

Ms McClure said she was "overcome with emotion seeing what they both had achieved" when their designs were paraded on the catwalk at Melbourne Exhibition Centre.

But that may be the end of their catwalk career.

Asked if we will see Ms McClure at Paris or London fashion weeks, she laughingly responds: "No, I'm too old for that."

World.title: Lakers lose 'MVP candidate' to injury as NBA play-offs approach
World.content:
Luka Dončić will miss the rest of the Los Angeles Lakers' regular season with a grade-two hamstring strain.

Dončić is the NBA's top scorer and the driving force behind the Lakers' surge into the third spot in the Western Conference standings.

But he injured his left leg during the Lakers' blowout 139-96 loss to Oklahoma City Thunder on Friday AEDT.

An MRI exam revealed the severity of the strain and an initial prognosis suggests Dončić will be sidelined indefinitely.

"At this point, at this juncture of the season, it's the last thing you want to see," Dončić's teammate LeBron James said.

"When you have an MVP candidate on your team, the last thing you want to see is somebody go down with a hamstring injury."

Dončić trade 'a seismic event in NBA history' Luka Dončić's controversial move from the Dallas Mavericks to the Los Angeles Lakers shook the NBA's foundations. Here is why the stunning move has such widespread ramifications.

Dončić was injured in the first half against the Thunder but was cleared to return to the game.

He lasted only about four minutes before he spun, stopped and went down on the court in pain, leading to his departure.

The Lakers (50-27 win-loss record) have just five games left before the post-season.

Grade-two hamstring strains sometimes require several weeks of recovery, but Dončić has experience with similar injuries.

He missed four games before the All-Star break with another left hamstring strain but returned to the Lakers line-up after the season resumed.

Dončić is putting up spectacular numbers in his first full season with the Lakers, who acquired the Slovenian star from the Mavericks last season.

He is averaging 33.5 points, 8.3 assists and 7.7 rebounds per game.

The 27-year-old was named the NBA's Western Conference player of the month for March after racking up 13 consecutive 30-point performances including seven 40-point games.

AP

World.title: 'Extraordinary' images of home as astronauts head towards moon
World.content:
The Artemis II astronauts have captured our blue planet's brilliant beauty as they zoom ever closer to the moon.

NASA has released initial images taken from inside the Orion spacecraft as the crew — commander Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen — forge ahead with their lunar mission.

One photo taken by commander Wiseman shows a curved slice of Earth in one of the capsule's windows.

The crew says: "The views are extraordinary." (AP: NASA)

The second shows the entire globe with the oceans topped by swirling white tendrils of clouds.

A green aurora even glows, according to NASA.

"It's great to think that — with the exception of our four friends — all of us are represented in this image," said NASA's Lakiesha Hawkins, an exploration systems leader back on the ground.

She added the mission was going well.

In pictures: Artemis II NASA's first mission to the Moon in decades For the first time in more than 50 years NASA has sent astronauts around the Moon, marking a major milestone in a new era of space exploration.

The three Americans and one Canadian will swing around the moon in their Orion capsule, hang a U-turn and then head straight back home without stopping.

They have fired Orion's main engine, setting them on their course.

After Mission Control Center shifted the position of their capsule, the entire Earth complete with northern lights filled their windows.

"It was the most spectacular moment, and it paused all four of us in our tracks," commander Wiseman said.

The crew members were able to catch their breath, and have taken part in a Q&A session with the press.

The Artemis II crew (from left): Canadian astronaut and mission specialist Jeremy Hansen, commander Reid Wiseman, mission specialist Christina Koch and pilot Victor Glover. (AP: NASA)

Jeremy Hansen told reporters: "There has been a tremendous amount of disbelief for me, it's just so extraordinary. I really like it up here.

"The views are extraordinary."

"It's really fun to be floating around" in zero gravity, he added.

"It just makes me feel like a little kid."

The crew members are the first lunar travellers since Apollo 17 in 1972.

The Artemis II mission is part of a longer-term plan to repeatedly return to the moon, with the goal of establishing a permanent lunar base that will offer a platform for further exploration.

AP/AFP

World.title: How do you clean a toilet brush and when should you change it?
World.content:
When was the last time you changed your toilet brush?

If you're just shoving the brush into its holder to wait for the next use — and actively avoiding thinking about how dirty the whole concept of it is — you're not alone.

Cleaning business owner Jason Shipway from Bunbury, Western Australia, on the traditional lands of the Noongar people, says the majority of toilet brushes he comes across when cleaning people's homes are "pretty gross".

"There's this massive bacteria biome just festering in the toilet-brush holder," he says.

Here's how often you should be changing your toilet brush, and how to make sure it's as hygienic as possible while it lasts.

Do toilet brushes harbour bacteria?

According to Helen Stratton, associate professor of microbiology at Griffith University, any bacteria or viruses that pass through the gut can end up on the toilet brush.

"If someone's ill, it's probably going to end up on the toilet brush, like with a virus, with any gastroenteritis or gastroenteric disease, that pathogen will be potentially on the toilet brush," she says.

If a toilet brush is not cleaned, it may introduce more germs into the toilet, Helen Stratton says. (Supplied)

That includes common illness-inducing bacteria such as E. coli and enterococci.

The main risk of contamination comes from these pathogens spraying onto other surfaces in the bathroom when the brush is moved between the toilet bowl and the brush holder, Ms Stratton says.

"If you're not careful, you're splashing that water around during the transfer from the toilet to the brush holder and vice versa," she says.

" That's really easy for the next person then to pick that up from the contamination around the seat or the floor or the wall, wherever it ends up. "

She notes it's especially important to minimise contamination if there are any immunocompromised people, elderly people or children living in the household.

"[A child's] immune system is not as mature as an adult … and they're at that height of the toilet seat."

How often should you change a toilet brush?

There are some telltale signs to look out for that indicate a toilet brush needs to be replaced, Mr Shipway says.

"If the bristles are fraying and it's visibly discoloured and it's not coming out with a soak with some bleach or a disinfectant, then it's probably a good sign that you should get rid of it."

Cleaning business owner Jason Shipway says it's important not to leave your toilet brush soaking wet between uses. (Supplied: Jason Shipway)

Traditional bristle brushes made of nylon and plastic should ideally be updated every three to six months, Mr Shipway says, whereas silicone brushes may last up to two years in use.

Ms Stratton recommends replacing toilet brushes every 6-12 months, but she also notes that it may depend on the material.

Silicone brushes are more hygienic than the common bristle brushes, which means they could last longer before needing replacing, she says.

"The bristle brushes, they're actually quite porous. And those pores are big enough for bacteria, viruses and even protozoa to sit in and accumulate," she explains.

"The silicone ones are much better because … the surface of the silica isn't something that bacteria and other microbes will attach to easily, so they stay physically cleaner. You're going to get less transfer of the material in the toilet bowl back onto those."

While silicone brushes may be slightly more expensive than plastic ones, Mr Shipway says they're worth it in the long run.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

What is the best way to clean a toilet brush?

It's a good idea to keep the brush down in the toilet bowl and clean it with a water flush to rinse off some of the contaminants after each use, Ms Stratton says.

On top of that, she recommends giving the brush a more thorough clean at least weekly or monthly, depending on how busy your household is.

"Glove up and give it a good wash in the laundry. Hot water is the best," Ms Stratton says.

"If you can even tip a bit of boiling water on or let it sit in boiling water and a bit of disinfectant."

If it's not cleaned between uses, she says the brush could easily bring more germs into the toilet.

" You're just inoculating the bowl again. You'll get rid of what you can see, but we can't see microbes without a microscope. "

Another hygiene factor to consider is the container that the brush sits in after use.

A wet toilet brush sitting in a contained holder is the perfect place for bacteria to grow, Ms Stratton says.

"If you don't have a disinfectant in there, if you're not cleaning the brush before you put it back in, it's moist. So, things can grow, that's their favourite environment."

The best way to clean the inside of your microwave When was the last time you cleaned your microwave? According to experts, it's actually a lot simpler than cleaning other appliances.

Instead, she recommends a holder that doesn't accumulate liquid but allows the brush to air dry.

"Most microbes and particularly human pathogens don't like to be dried out, they'll die. That's one way of reducing that risk of contamination further down the track."

If you do have a toilet-brush holder that accumulates liquid, Ms Stratton recommends adding and regularly replacing a disinfectant to counteract pathogen growth inside the holder.

But even if you do that, Mr Shipman says it's crucial to let the brush dry between each use.

"Sandwich it between the toilet and the seat and then just let it dry for about 10 to 15 minutes."

World.title: Demons star praised for reaching 'another level' with career-best form
World.content:
Ed Langdon says Melbourne teammate Kysaiah Pickett has "taken his game to another level", as the Demons continue life under new coach Steven King.

Pickett has relished greater midfield time with some career-best numbers, averaging 22.7 disposals, 4.3 clearances and 5.3 tackles per match this season.

The explosive 24-year-old produced a brilliant second-half performance in Melbourne's comeback win over Carlton at the MCG last Sunday.

Voss unfazed about speculation over his future Michael Voss knows he faces more scrutiny over his role as Blues coach after his side endures another second-half meltdown.

The Demons' victory gave the club a 2-1 (win-loss) start to their campaign.

"He's certainly taken his game to another level," Langdon said of Pickett.

"He's such a terrific player and he's focusing more and more on his midfield craft, and working out how the best midfielders in the competition go about it.

"And we know what he can do when he goes forward — that's kicking goals."

The Demons face Gold Coast at the MCG on Sunday afternoon.

Prior to the start of the season, Demons players had one eye on this clash as it was set to be their first meeting with ex-teammate Christian Petracca.

Petracca joined the Suns during last year's trade period, ending an 11-year stint at the Demons, with whom he won the 2021 premiership.

Christian Petracca is sidelined with a hamstring injury. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Matt Roberts)

But Petracca will miss Sunday's match because of a hamstring injury, robbing the encounter of its main attraction.

"It's a shame. It would've been great to play against Christian," Langdon said.

"But he's had an unbelievable start to the year, so it might benefit us that he's actually not playing."

The Demons have recalled Daniel Turner and veteran forward Jake Melksham, with Changkuoth Jiath (calf) and Paddy Cross (thumb) both ruled out because of injury.

Petracca and suspended forward Bailey Humphrey are missing for the Suns.

But Suns coach Damien Hardwick welcomes back Brownlow Medal winner Matt Rowell from injury to bolster his midfield.

AAP

World.title: After decades of success, love and loss, outback pub changes hands
World.content:
Standing on the front deck of the watering hole he turned into an outback icon, Stephen "Burnsie" Burns leans on the shoulders of Tom Leggett.

After 24 years at the helm of the Nindigully Pub, Burnsie is leasing the business to the 39 -year-old navy veteran.

"The Gully" is one of Queensland's oldest pubs. Its first license dates back to 1864. (Supplied: Nindigully Pub)

During his time calling the shots, Burnsie made it his mission to turn the Gully, about 500 kilometres west of Brisbane, into a must-visit tourism destination.

It proved a smart business model for a town with just nine permanent residents.

The venue's position on the bank of the Moonie River, free camping, country music events, oversized meals and commitment to genuine hospitality have seen it win multiple tourism awards, including Queensland's best outback pub in 2019.

Sunshine Coast locals Marty and Lisa Petersen said stopping the Nindigully Pub was a highlight of their outback holiday. (ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura)

Reflecting on his time at the helm, the former Sunshine Coast builder said he never planned on owning a pub "in the middle of nowhere".

"I bought it emotionally, because I loved the pub," Burnsie said.

"The river, the Australian architecture."

He recalled the state the building was in in 2002 a little less fondly.

"It was a heap of shit," Burnsie said.

" The worst pub you ever walked into. "

The Gully's renovated beer garden can hold up to 3,500 people. (Supplied: Nindigully Pub)

'Pissant pub in the middle of nowhere'

Burnsie said his brother, with whom he shared a construction business, laughed at the purchase at the time.

"He said, 'I can't believe you bought a pissant pub in the middle of nowhere for the amount of money you make in a year,'" he said.

"I said, 'Life's not always about money.'"

Over the years, Burnsie reconstructed the flooring, rebuilt the bar and kitchen, replaced the old plumbing and, perhaps most notably, painted the exterior several times.

The pub was painted pink in 2012 to raise money and awareness for breast cancer, a cause close to Burnsie's heart after losing two wives to cancer during his time as owner.

The pub was painted pink in 2012 to raise money and awareness for breast cancer. (Supplied: Nindigully Pub)

He said his second wife Deb was the driving force behind the resurgence of the Nindigully Pub.

"It never really did anything until she got here," he said.

As well as being the energy and intelligence behind the operation, Burnsie credited Deb with reining in some of his more outlandish ideas.

"I wanted to do V8 super cow racing, long-neck Indian duck racing, esky racing with little motors on the back," he said.

"She said, 'That's stupid — people will get hurt.'

"About half the ideas she'd say no to — but then you'd get a yes and we'd run with the yeses."

One of those ideas became the pub's flagship annual event, the Nindigully Pig Races, which now attracts thousands of visitors and has raised hundreds of thousands of dollars for the Royal Flying Doctor Service.

Stephen Burns credits Deb with building the pub into the icon it is today. (Supplied: Nindigully Pub)

Deb died four years ago, but her presence remains strongly felt.

Her name appears on the licence board above the threshold, her photograph hangs in the bar and she rests in a rose garden on the pub's grounds.

Burnsie said Deb was the reason he stayed on for so long.

"We worked together on a plan of what we wanted to achieve, particularly in the beer garden," he said.

"What you see now is what we wanted to get to."

He said he was not prepared to lease or step away from the establishment until that vision had been completed.

'Like no other place on earth'

With Deb's dream realised, Burnsie has handed over the reins to Mr Leggett, who first arrived as a patron.

"I made the mistake of fixing something and became friends with Burnsie," Mr Leggett said.

Tom Leggett admits managing an outback pub wasn't something he aspired to, but he fell in love with the place just as Burnsie had. (ABC Southern Qld: Dan McCray)

After repairing a broken quad bike, Mr Leggett was invited to stay on longer, eventually becoming Burnsie's "apprentice".

Two years later, after some hard work and a deep dive into the business figures, he took over the lease.

Mr Leggett, who spent eight years in the navy and is a qualified diesel mechanic and electrical fitter, admits running the pub wasn't on his "bucket list", but that didn't dampen his enthusiasm.

"I've got big goals but they're probably a next-year problem," he said.

Mr Leggett said he shared the same reverence for the venue as its long-time publican.

"It's like no other place on earth," he said.

Stephen Burns followed his heart and bought the Nindigully Pub in 2002. (ABC Southern Qld: Dan McCray)

As for Burnsie, he plans to spend his retirement with his V8 cars and growing collection of motorcycles at the house he built behind the pub.

When asked about the future, his answer was characteristically blunt.

"I'll be dead in five years," he said.

World.title: More people are using this 'secret deal' to get an EV. Here's what to know
World.content:
With eye-watering prices at the petrol bowser hurting wallets, more Australians than ever are looking at purchasing an electric vehicle.

For some, novated leases are like a "secret deal", allowing them to sacrifice part of their salary to get an EV with no up-front cost — while also saving them thousands in taxes.

But the mechanism is not for everyone, and some major traps could unravel all the benefits, leaving you in a worse position.

While everyone is advised to speak with an accountant to see if a novated lease is right for them, here is some general information to get you started.

What is a novated lease?

A novated lease is essentially a three-party agreement between yourself, your employer and a leasing company.

Instead of using cash or a loan to buy a car, a novated lease involves you sacrificing part of your salary to pay for both the vehicle and its running costs.

Track the latest petrol and diesel prices around Australia See what's happening with petrol and diesel prices near you, updated constantly.

As a simplified example, let's say you are buying a $40,000 car, which will also cost about $8,000 for four years of running costs (registration, insurance, maintenance, etc).

Under a novated lease, you might agree to drop your salary by $12,000 annually for four years to make those payments.

That is generally the gist of things, though payments will also vary depending on interest rates, fees and residual value.

The big drawcard is that the payments for a novated lease will come out of your salary pre-tax.

How does it save you money?

The simplest way to think about it is that by reducing your salary, you are now reducing the amount of money the government can tax you.

The money you are giving up from your income is all going directly to the leasing company, before the Australian Tax Office can get its hands on some of it.

Rohan Martin is the chief executive of the National Automotive Leasing and Salary Packaging Association (NALSPA), which advocates for the novated lease sector.

He said the mechanism helps with "putting more money into your pocket".

"With a novated lease, there are no up-front costs, everything can be bundled into a fortnightly payment," Mr Martin said.

" Also with a novated lease, you avoid GST (goods and services tax) on both the car's purchase price and running costs. "

What happens at the end of the lease?

At the end of a novated lease, you do not automatically own the car.

Instead, there is usually a residual value — a final lump sum that must be paid if you want to keep the vehicle.

Mr Martin said people can typically either pay out the residual to take full ownership of the car, sell the vehicle and use the proceeds to cover the remaining amount, or roll the lease into a new agreement.

How popular is it?

One of the big catches with a novated lease is that your employer is made to pay a fringe benefits tax (FBT), which they will often then pass on to their employee.

Mr Martin said for a $60,000 vehicle, the FBT might cost someone more than $5,000 a year, which would eat into a large chunk of the savings they are making on tax.

However, electric vehicles that satisfy certain criteria have been exempt from FBT since July 2022.

That exemption transformed the novated lease from a niche scheme with questionable benefits into a genuine money-saving option for a large percentage of Australians.

Electric vehicles getting cheaper The price tag of EVs has been a barrier to uptake. As cheaper models hit the market, will more drivers go electric?

NALSPA estimates there are more than 500,000 people using novated leases to pay off their car — a figure which it says is "growing quickly".

Mr Martin said there had been a material jump in interest over the past month, due to the rising cost of fuel.

"We've seen a significant uptake and interest in novated leases, particularly around electric vehicles," he said.

"We're seeing many motorists, particularly those who are living further out from the CBD … looking at novated leasing and the EV discount as a way to get them into a far more affordable vehicle."

Interest in novated leases for electric vehicles has been rising since the conflict in the Middle East started increasing petrol prices. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

Are there any negatives?

Independent consumer advocate Chang-Yang Yew has two vehicles through novated leases and runs a website where he shares his knowledge about the scheme.

Tax-saving car deals have long-term costs Trying to reduce her taxable income ended up costing Tara Byrne thousands of dollars in the long run.

"When this is used appropriately, it's pretty much an amazing deal," Mr Yew said.

"It's almost like a secret deal … and you feel like you want to share it with your friends and family."

One of his main focuses is alerting people to "misleading practices" by novated leasing companies.

"I deem myself as someone who is passionate about justice, which is why a lot of what I do is trying to tell people what to watch out for," Mr Yew said.

"Lots of people are trapped in this commitment, which is clearly not appropriate for them, because of all the caveats and traps."

Chang-Yang Yew runs a website where he shares his knowledge of novated leases with people. (Supplied: Chang-Yang Yew)

Changing jobs can cause the deal to collapse

Mr Yew said the "main trap" with novated leases was that the agreement was linked to your continued employment with the same company.

If you are made redundant or change jobs to an employer that does not support novated leasing, your entire deal can collapse.

"All your leftover lease commitments now have to be paid out in full … and they have to be paid out with the [full] amount … so you lose all your tax-related savings," he said.

" The loss may be that you end up paying more for the car compared to paying for the car with cash in the first place, in some cases. "

Changing jobs could result in your novated lease collapsing, if your new employer doesn't allow the scheme. (ABC News: Jess Davis)

Mr Martin agreed that this was something people should seriously consider before signing up for a novated lease.

"If, for whatever reason, the new employer didn't enable you to transfer that lease, then there may be break costs associated with the novated lease," he said.

" You need to be careful or mindful of that if your employment is about to change. "

Impact on borrowing capacity

Why fuel prices could go much higher Trying to guess exactly where the oil price tops out is fast becoming the chocolate wheel of choice among politicians, economists and oil experts.

If you are looking to take out a home loan in the next few years, having a novated lease can significantly impact your borrowing capacity.

Mr Yew said, in some cases, the decrease can be roughly three times the value of your car.

In that situation, a novated lease for a $50,000 vehicle could drop your borrowing capacity by $150,000.

"This could be trouble for people who are trying to get on the property ladder, because they're trying to get a car for five years," he said.

On the flip side, a novated lease can provide a double benefit if you already own a house.

Not only do you pay less tax, but the lack of an up-front payment could allow you to put more money in your home loan's offset account, reducing your interest payments.

Limited choice can mean higher costs

An issue to be aware of is that not all employees have the freedom to shop around for the best deal.

Some companies have exclusive arrangements with a single novated lease provider, meaning workers are effectively locked into using that company.

Mr Yew said this lack of competition can result in higher effective interest rates and fees, because employees do not have alternate providers to compare against.

In those situations, he said the "tax savings" promoted by leasing companies may not reflect the full picture.

Mr Yew compared it to a supermarket raising the price of a chocolate bar before advertising a discount, highlighting the saving without drawing attention to the higher starting cost.

He said that, where possible, employees should check whether their workplace allows multiple providers, which can make it easier to secure a better deal.

Any other risks?

Another risk with novated leases is what happens if you are involved in a serious crash that writes off the car.

Mr Yew said that if your insurance plan doesn't provide enough funds or a replacement vehicle, this could result in your lease being terminated through an accelerated payout.

He also said that if you are using a novated lease to get an electric vehicle, which is exempt from FBTs, this can result in your adjusted taxable income (ATI) increasing.

Some companies have exclusive arrangements with novated lease providers, meaning employees aren't able to shop around for the best deals. (ABC News: Brendan Esposito)

This can result in your government subsidies, such as for child care or child support, being reduced, and your higher education repayments being increased.

Mr Yew said employers are also permitted to reduce your superannuation payments to reflect your lowered salary on a novated lease, though most companies do not do this.

So, should I get a novated lease?

There is no one-size-fits-all answer — with both Mr Yew and Mr Martin agreeing that the benefits depend heavily on your personal circumstances.

For higher-income earners with stable jobs and a house, particularly those not planning to change employers, a novated lease on an eligible EV can deliver significant savings.

But the same structure can work against people in less stable situations.

Whether or not a novated lease is right for you can depend on a variety of factors. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Mr Yew said people should carefully consider factors such as job security, future plans to change employers, and whether they are trying to enter the housing market.

He also pointed to the potential downsides, including reduced borrowing capacity, possible impacts on government benefits, and the risk of having to pay out early.

Mr Martin said people should treat novated leasing like any other financial commitment and ensure they understand all the obligations involved.

Both recommend seeking independent financial advice before signing up, rather than relying solely on estimates provided by leasing companies.

How do I get one?

If you've read all this and want to barrel ahead, the first step is to check whether your employer offers novated leasing.

Mr Martin said most medium and large organisations will already have arrangements in place with leasing providers, while others may allow employers to choose their own.

Once approved, a leasing provider typically organises the finance, vehicle purchase and running cost estimates, which are then bundled into regular payroll deductions.

While the approval process is generally quick, potentially only taking a few days, the biggest delay can be when the vehicle itself is available.

Once again, it is advised that you seek independent financial advice before making any major agreements.

World.title: One day, I may need to figure out how to get pregnant
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessFertility Opinion One day, I may need to figure out how to get pregnant Chanel Contos Founder of Teach Us Consent April 4, 2026 — 10:00am

April 4, 2026 — 10:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

It took me until my mid-20s to properly understand my menstrual cycle and what each phase meant for my mind and body. Not because I wasn’t curious or feeling the effects of them, but because learning about women’s bodies tends to happen reactively – after confusion, discomfort or something going wrong. Over many moons, I paid careful attention to moods, cravings, discharge, pain and energy. Eventually, I pieced together how my hormones were affecting my mind and body (for better and for worse). It may have taken over a decade of menstruating, but I now know my body well enough to clock ovulation from the smallest cramp, and understand that a 10-hour sleep accompanied by a change in the smell of my right underarm (I wish I was kidding) means my luteal phase has commenced. Fertility education: Chanel Contos says even though she is many years away from making a decision about having children “I’m insistent that I will not be met with complete confusion and disorientation when I do”. All of this awareness, laboriously acquired, has so far been used to achieve my to-date life’s most important mission: to not get pregnant. But as more of my friends enter a new era of life, I’m realising that one day, I may need to figure out how to get pregnant. Given how much fear has been ingrained in me about how easy it is to have an unwanted pregnancy, I assumed to plan one must be as simple as 1+1, but that’s not always the case. This incomplete information about what goes into the process of getting pregnant isn’t a personal failure, but instead the product of decades of underfunded research, poor education and a millennia-old stigma surrounding women’s bodies.



What I’m experiencing isn’t unique, it’s reflected in national data. Australia’s fertility rate is and has been in decline for decades, driven by delayed parenthood, economic uncertainty, changing social norms and youth disengagement, all contributing to a growing gap between fertility intentions and outcomes for young Australians. Related Article Fertility The fertility conversation we are missing in our teens and 20s All these factors compound to create a national fertility literacy gap, meaning that most Australian women don’t begin learning about fertility until they start “trying”, or considering their options once it’s found to be not seamless. Why are we encouraged to learn about fertility only once it becomes urgent? And why haven’t we learnt the lesson of the necessity to be proactive in understanding women’s bodies to ensure greater control, better health outcomes and greater decision-making capabilities? I am unsure if you’re meant to feel unequivocally confident about a decision as life-altering as wanting children. If you are, I’m not there yet, but it feels unfair that the uncertainty many face is compounded by missing information. The only thing I am certain my future self will want is options, and to truly choose, information and understanding is needed. As we begrudgingly know, age is the most important factor affecting a woman’s chances of having a baby. However, it’s become news to me recently that the infamous “35” number is not the turning point, but that fertility gradually declines in your late 20s, and then even more quickly in your late 30s.



Fertility (more specifically infertility) is still largely perceived as a “women’s” issue, and unsuccessful attempts at conception can still come with implicit social stigma. This belief reflects historical attitudes that defined women primarily through their reproductive role, with challenges conceiving often misunderstood or unfairly individualised. We now know that male fertility and sperm quality decline with age as well, and (I hope we all know) that women’s lives and identities are not defined by their capacity to reproduce. Related Article Fertility This at-home ‘egg timer’ test is an Aussie first. What does it tell us about fertility? Yet most fertility conversations still happen too late, acting as a means to solve a problem, triggered by difficulty conceiving, declining numbers or fear. We are yet to take a strength-based approach and incorporate fertility education as part of lifelong health outcomes. I am many years out from making a decision about children, but I’m insistent that I will not be met with complete confusion and disorientation when I do. So, I’m now choosing to understand my fertility health. Not because I want answers about babies, but because I want answers about my body. I absolutely love knowing what’s going on inside me. I’m that patient who makes the doctor go through every line of the blood test, even if the results are normal, to better understand. From a material perspective, I’ve had similar tests conducted before, but they were to identify a problem and try to help solve it. Being in the waiting room, and then the chair this time, felt different. It wasn’t scary the way it’s been in the past. I think this is because I wasn’t anticipating the Catch-22 of either a diagnosis or no answer in the results. Rather, I was taking charge of my own body and was simply gathering more information to be used however I wanted.



For some, the first step in their fertility journey may be as simple as adding in a short conversation about fertility health as part of routine check-up care. Depending on what your GP recommends, this may mean follow-up appointments or various tests to reveal information about your specific questions. Conversations about fertility health shouldn’t be to encourage people to have children earlier, or at all, but instead to gather more information for better-informed decisions. Nothing to do with our bodies can ever be certain or absolute, but the earlier we start considering the options, then at least whatever choice we make in the future will be properly informed. Chanel Contos is founder and chief executive of Teach Us Consent and author of Consent Laid Bare. She is now a Governor Phillip Scholar at Oxford University, studying public policy. World.title: If a Wallabies team was picked today, here’s who should be in it
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Opinion If a Wallabies team was picked today, here’s who should be in it Paul Cully Rugby columnist April 4, 2026 — 9:33am

April 4, 2026 — 9:33am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Wallabies coach Joe Schmidt might lean forward a bit more in his seat during Super Rugby this weekend. After seven rounds, the Waratahs are effectively entering their version of the playoffs, Zac Lomax is poised to debut off the bench for the Western Force, and Will Skelton’s Achilles injury has left an enormous gap in the Wallabies’ pack. Loading Skelton confirmed this week that his French season is over, raising grave doubts about whether he’ll play for the Wallabies this year. The Waratahs’ trip to Hamilton has a finals feel because Dan McKellar’s side can’t afford to drop too far behind in the race for the top six. But a win would completely change the complexion of their season: the game against the Chiefs is consequential.



If the Waratahs respond to that pressure, Schmidt will take note. He has a few gaps to fill in his first Wallabies squad of the year, and he might also be looking for a few well-established players to step up this weekend. Charlie Cale has made a great start to 2026. Getty Images Harry Wilson, in particular, is under pressure from Brumbies No.8 Charlie Cale. Despite a heavy workload, there is no sign yet that Cale is dropping off in form or shirking the close-quarters stuff.



In the tight five, James Slipper has retired, Angus Bell is up at Ulster, and Taniela Tupou is having limited impact at Racing 92, having made only seven appearances since his move to France – the majority off the bench. As a result, Waratahs props Dan Botha and Tom Lambert, as well as Reds midfielder Isaac Henry, must be under consideration after significantly raising their performance levels this season. Dan Botha on the charge for the Waratahs. Getty Images Unlike Cale, they have not been capped, but the quartet could all be classed as newcomers given the amount of rugby the Brumbies No.8 has missed due to injury. A lot can change between now and July, but based on current form and availability the Wallabies have some new options to consider a year before the Rugby World Cup.



Paul Cully’s Wallabies team 1. Tom Lambert (Waratahs): The 25-year-old is morphing into a very good, mobile prop and his best years are ahead of him. Wallabies can’t afford to lose the Scotland-qualified loosehead through lack of opportunity. 2. Billy Pollard (Brumbies): An established Wallaby now, although the Reds’ Josh Nasser is pushing hard, and competition in that spot is increasing. 3. Dan Botha (Waratahs): A great name for a tighthead prop, and he has definitely brought some Springboks-like toughness to his work around the field. 4. Matt Philip (Waratahs): A revelation since his return to Super Rugby, although Jeremy Williams is also playing well at the Force and Nick Frost will come into the picture as the season progresses.



5. Lukhan Salakaia-Loto (Reds): Skelton’s absence means the Wallabies are crying out for an enforcer, and Salakaia-Loto is currently the best option. 6. Rob Valetini (Brumbies): The Brumbies back-rower remains the best ball carrier in the whole competition. Rob Valetini was immense for the Brumbies against NSW last week. Getty Images 7. Fraser McReight (Reds): McReight and Force No.7 Carlo Tizzano have not been at their best, but their class is unquestionable. 8. Charlie Cale (Brumbies): The big mover in Super Rugby this year. He can carry in tight spaces and use his speed on the edge, emerging as a genuine rival to Harry Wilson.



9. Ryan Lonergan (Brumbies): The conductor in Canberra, although Jake Gordon’s excellent performance in the Waratahs’ win last weekend felt like a statement. 10. Carter Gordon (Reds): Injuries have held him back again. However, when fit, he gives the Reds an extra dimension. Carter Gordon has been flying high for the Reds in 2026. Getty Images 11. Max Jorgensen (Waratahs): A world-class operator who does something special almost every weekend. 12. Hunter Paisami (Reds): Len Ikitau and Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii will presumably be the preferred combination when fit, but Ikitau last played for Exeter in December and Suaalii is still recovering from his hamstring injury.



13. Isaac Henry (Reds): The 27-year-old has overcome some terrible luck with injury and is impressing with his speed and running lines. Related Article Australian rugby Australia push for reform to ‘crazy’ transfer system after securing young strongman 14. Dylan Pietsch (Force): Makes his return from injury against the Reds on Saturday. It is easy to forget the impact he was starting to make at the Wallabies last year before he was sidelined. His physicality sets him apart. 15. Jock Campbell (Reds): Tom Wright’s return from an ACL injury will be closely watched, but Campbell has put up his hand. Replacements: Josh Nasser (Reds), Angus Bell (Ulster), Tom Robertson (Force), Jeremy Williams (Force), Tom Hooper (Exeter), Jake Gordon (Waratahs), Noah Lolesio (Shuttles Aichi), Filipo Daugunu (Reds) Watch every match of Super Rugby Pacific live and exclusive on Stan Sport.

We are yet to take a strength-based approach and incorporate fertility education as part of lifelong health outcomes. So, I’m now choosing to understand my fertility health. Not because I want answers about babies, but because I want answers about my body. I absolutely love knowing what’s going on inside me. I’m that patient who makes the doctor go through every line of the blood test, even if the results are normal, to better understand. From a material perspective, I’ve had similar tests conducted before, but they were to identify a problem and try to help solve it. Being in the waiting room, and then the chair this time, felt different. It wasn’t scary the way it’s been in the past. I think this is because I wasn’t anticipating the Catch-22 of either a diagnosis or no answer in the results. Rather, I was taking charge of my own body and was simply gathering more information to be used however I wanted.



For some, the first step in their fertility journey may be as simple as adding in a short conversation about fertility health as part of routine check-up care. Depending on what your GP recommends, this may mean follow-up appointments or various tests to reveal information about your specific questions. Conversations about fertility health shouldn’t be to encourage people to have children earlier, or at all, but instead to gather more information for better-informed decisions. Nothing to do with our bodies can ever be certain or absolute, but the earlier we start considering the options, then at least whatever choice we make in the future will be properly informed. Chanel Contos is founder and chief executive of Teach Us Consent and author of Consent Laid Bare. She is now a Governor Phillip Scholar at Oxford University, studying public policy. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.
